For as long as I've been brewing, the process has always been a mix of equal parts science, patience, and a fair bit of trial and error. It's a rewarding journey, but as the experiments get more ambitious and the batches more frequent, the costs of quality ingredients—honey, yeast, grains, and fruits—start to add up.

To keep the momentum going and accelerate the pace of these experiments, I've decided to open up a way for those of you who enjoy the recipes and findings to contribute.

Why Support the Brew?

Brewing isn't just about following a recipe; it's about the pursuit of the perfect profile. To get there, I'm constantly testing different variables: varying honey sources, experimenting with nutrient timings, and trying out unique fruit additions.

By helping cover the cost of ingredients, you're directly fueling this research. My goal is to push the boundaries of what's possible in a home setup and, most importantly, to share every single finding—the triumphs and the "learning experiences"—with all of you.

What Your Support Enables

Every contribution goes directly back into the carboys. Specifically, your support helps with:

  • Quality Ingredients: Sourcing higher-grade honey and specialized yeast strains.
  • Diverse Experiments: Trying out expensive fruits or rare additives that I might otherwise skip.
  • Consistent Documentation: Allowing me to dedicate more time to outlining the findings and sharing detailed guides here on the blog.

How to Contribute

If you'd like to help keep the fermentation flowing, you can support me via Ko-fi:

Support the Brewing Journey on Ko-fi

Whether it's the cost of a single jar of honey or a larger contribution to a complex batch, every bit makes a tangible difference in how quickly we can test new theories and share the results.

Thank you for being part of this journey and for supporting the craft. Let's see what we can brew next.

Pasteurization is one way to stop fermentation without adding potassium metabisulfite or potassium sorbate. The idea is simple: after you back sweeten or bottle condition, you gently heat the mead until the yeast are killed, then cool it quickly. Once the yeast are dead, the sweetness and carbonation level are locked in.

When Pasteurization Makes Sense

Pasteurization is useful when you want a sweet or sparkling mead but do not want to use chemical stabilizers. It also matters for carbonated mead because once priming sugar is in the bottle, fermentation will keep going until either the sugar runs out or the yeast stop. If you want a specific sweetness and a controlled level of carbonation, you need a way to halt the yeast at the right moment.

This step can happen before or after bottling. Some brewers pasteurize the entire batch in a fermenter, then bottle a stable mead. Others bottle first, let the mead carbonate to the desired level, then pasteurize the sealed bottles. Both approaches work.

Chemical Stabilization as an Alternative

If you do not want to use heat at all, the most common alternative is a combination of potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate. The metabisulfite knocks down the yeast population and helps protect the mead from oxidation, while the sorbate prevents any surviving yeast cells from reproducing. I wait about 24 to 48 hours after adding them, then back-sweeten to taste. Once the sweetness is stable, I bottle the still mead without worrying about refermentation.

I use chemical stabilization when I want precise control over the final sweetness and when I am bottling still mead in corked or swing-top bottles. Pasteurization and chemical stabilization do the same job in different ways; which one you choose depends on your equipment, your preference for sulfites, and whether the mead is still or carbonated.

My Preferred Heat Method

I prefer to pasteurize using heat, and I do it before bottling. I put my one-gallon fermenter directly into my brewing kettle, fill the kettle with water up to the level of the mead inside the fermenter, and heat the water slowly. This gives me an even, gentle heat around the fermenter rather than direct heat on the glass or plastic.

I raise the temperature of the mead to about 140°F and hold it there for roughly 20 minutes. A probe thermometer makes it easy to watch the internal temperature without opening the fermenter. After the hold, I lift the fermenter out and let it cool, or transfer the mead to a sanitized vessel once it is at a safe temperature.

Doing it this way means I do not have to handle dozens of individual bottles in a hot water bath, and I do not have to run multiple small batches through the kettle. It also avoids the risk of a bottle cracking or seal failing during heating because the pasteurization happens in a single sturdy fermenter.

Important Details

Use a fermenter that can handle warm water and moderate temperature swings. A glass carboy or stainless fermenter is ideal. Thin plastic may deform or leach flavors, so check the temperature rating of your vessel before trying this.

Heat the water slowly. Rushing the temperature can shock the fermenter or drive off aromatics from the mead. I aim for a few degrees per minute, not a rapid climb.

Watch the temperature closely. 140°F is a commonly cited target. Higher temperatures work, but you should shorten the hold time accordingly. Lower temperatures may not kill enough yeast unless you hold the mead there longer. Use a reliable thermometer and give the mead time to equalize throughout the vessel.

Note that you can also pasteurize at 160°F for about 1 minute, but I shy away from that. A shorter time at a higher temperature can still affect delicate flavors, and I prefer the gentler 140°F hold.

Cool the mead quickly once the hold is complete. I move the fermenter to a cool spot or set it in a bath of cool water. Fast cooling helps preserve aroma and reduces the chance of oxidation or continued heat exposure.

Pasteurizing Bottles

If you prefer to carbonate in the bottle and then pasteurize, the process is similar but the containers are smaller. You seal the bottles, let them carbonate at room temperature until they reach the pressure you want, then submerge them in a hot water bath. The water temperature should bring the liquid inside the bottle to around 140°F for the same short hold.

Use only bottles that can handle heat and pressure. Beer bottles, Champagne bottles, or heavy swing-tops are the safe choices. Thin wine bottles or decorative glass can crack or shatter. Always wear gloves and eye protection, and keep the bottles away from people and pets while they are hot.

Taste and Safety

Pasteurization, when done carefully, has very little impact on flavor. If you overshoot the temperature or hold too long, you can start to cook the mead or drive off delicate aromatics. Practice with water first if you are unsure of your setup, and take notes on temperature and timing so you can repeat it.

For my own batches, the kettle-and-fermenter method is the easiest and most consistent way to get a stable, sweet mead without sulfites or sorbates.

nodes.html:
Most meads ferment almost completely dry unless you intentionally stop the yeast early. A dry mead is not bad, but a lot of beginners expect something a little sweeter and are surprised when their first batch tastes sharp or thin. Back sweetening is the fix: you add a sweetener, usually honey, after fermentation is finished, and you do it slowly enough that you can taste the change between additions.

Before You Sweeten

Back sweetening only works safely if the yeast are no longer active. If fermentation is still going and you add honey, the yeast will simply ferment it away. There are two ways to handle this.

Wait for Fermentation to Finish

The simplest approach is to let the yeast finish naturally, confirm with stable gravity readings for two or three days, then sweeten. The risk is that any live yeast can restart if conditions change, so this works best if you plan to drink the mead quickly or keep it cold.

Stabilize First

The safest approach is to make sure the yeast cannot restart before you add honey. The most common way is covered in the next part of this series: a combination of potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate. You can also use heat pasteurization, which is covered there as well. Either way, stabilize before you sweeten, or your sweetness will keep fermenting away.

How I Add Honey

Honey is not just sugar. It carries flavor, aroma, body, and sometimes a little bitterness or spice depending on the variety. That means adding honey changes more than sweetness, and it is much easier to add more later than to remove too much. I add honey in small increments, usually a few ounces at a time for a one-gallon batch, then stir gently and taste.

I add honey in small increments, usually a few ounces at a time for a one-gallon batch, then gently mix it into the mead with a sanitized spoon and taste. I wait a minute or two between tastes so my palate resets. Once the sweetness feels balanced against the acid, tannin, and alcohol heat, I stop. The goal is balance, not a specific number.

A mead with more acidity or tannin can handle more sweetness without tasting syrupy. A very clean traditional mead might need less. Alcohol heat can also make a mead taste drier than it is, so a small amount of sweetness can smooth that out. Taste with that in mind. If the mead tastes hot or thin, a little honey can help. If it already tastes heavy or flabby, leave it alone.

I write down how much honey I added so I can reproduce the result next time. A notebook or brewing log is useful here because "a little more" is hard to remember.

My Take

I rarely back sweeten my meads. When I do, I add honey in small amounts, tasting between each addition, until the mead feels balanced. Once the sweetness is where I want it, I stabilize. With pasteurization, that means gently heating the mead to lock in the sweetness. With chemical stabilization, that means adding potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate and waiting before I bottle. Either way, the sweetness goes in before the final stability step.

Primary fermentation gets most of the attention because it is active, bubbly, and dramatic. But secondary fermentation is where a mead really starts to settle into something drinkable, and it is usually the longest phase of the whole process. In this seventh part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will explain what secondary fermentation is, why it lasts so long, and how I decide when a mead is ready to bottle.

What Secondary Fermentation Is

Secondary fermentation is the phase after you rack the mead off the primary yeast sediment, called the lees, into a clean vessel. It is much slower than primary. The yeast are still finishing their work, the mead is slowly clearing, and harsh flavors are beginning to mellow.

For me, secondary fermentation is also the conditioning and aging step. Once the mead is off the lees and in a clean vessel, it stays there for weeks or months while it clears and matures. I do not transfer it again into a separate "bulk aging" vessel. The secondary vessel is the conditioning and aging vessel.

Why Rack to Secondary

The main reason to move a mead off the lees is to avoid off-flavors. Yeast that sit in the sediment for too long can start to break down, releasing compounds that taste yeasty, bready, or even sulfury. Racking to a clean vessel removes the mead from most of that sediment and gives it a fresher environment to finish in.

Secondary also gives me a controlled place to add fruit, spices, oak, or other flavorings. When I add ingredients in secondary, I get more control over the flavor and color than I would in primary, and I can taste-test along the way.

Finally, the move to secondary begins the clearing process. As fermentation slows and yeast drop out of suspension, the mead gradually becomes bright and transparent. That clarity makes a big difference in how finished mead looks in the bottle.

When to Move to Secondary

I move a mead to secondary once gravity readings are stable for two or three days in a row. That tells me the yeast have mostly finished consuming sugar and are moving into cleanup mode. I do not move based on the airlock alone. Bubbles can slow or stop while the yeast are still working, so gravity is the more reliable signal.

I also look at the visual cues. The foam cap, if there was one, has fallen. The must looks less milky and more translucent. A thick layer of sediment has collected at the bottom of the fermenter. Those signs, combined with stable gravity, mean the timing is right.

The Racking Process

Before I touch the mead, I clean and sanitize the new vessel, the siphon or auto-siphon, any tubing, and the airlock. Everything that will contact the mead needs to be sanitized.

I place the primary fermenter on a counter or table and the secondary vessel on the floor below it. I start the siphon carefully so I do not stir up the sediment at the bottom. I stop before I pull any lees into the new vessel, even if that means leaving a little liquid behind. It is better to lose a cup of mead than to move a cup of yeast sludge into secondary.

If I am adding fruit, spices, or oak, I put them into the sanitized secondary vessel first and rack the mead on top. That helps distribute the additions and reduces the amount of splashing.

What Happens in Secondary

During secondary the mead continues to ferment very slowly if at all. Yeast that are still in suspension finish consuming remaining sugars and metabolize byproducts from primary. Harsh alcohol edges begin to soften. Suspended particles begin to settle out.

If I added fruit in secondary, color and flavor extract over the next one to four weeks. Berries usually give up most of their contribution within two weeks. Oak, spices, and herbs can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks depending on how strong I want them.

I check the airlock occasionally, but I do not expect much activity. A bubble every few minutes is normal. What I watch more closely is clarity and flavor.

How Long Secondary Takes

This is where patience matters. Secondary fermentation is not a two-week formality for me. It is the long conditioning and aging phase.

A light melomel might be reasonably clear and ready to bottle in four to six weeks. A traditional mead made with a strong honey like buckwheat might need three to six months. A high-alcohol sack mead can improve for a year or more.

I base the length on taste and clarity, not the calendar. I pull a sample every few weeks once the mead is stable. When the alcohol heat has softened, the flavors feel connected, and the mead looks clear enough, I start thinking about bottling. If it still tastes raw or aggressive, I wait.

Temperature also plays a role. A cool, stable room clears mead faster than a warm one because yeast drop out of suspension more readily. I keep my secondary vessels sealed, out of direct light, and at whatever stable room temperature I have.

When to Rack Again

Some batches need to be racked a second or third time if more sediment settles out after the first transfer. If a new layer of yeast, fruit particles, or other solids builds up at the bottom of the vessel, I rack again to keep the mead off the sediment.

You will particularly need a second racking if you added fruit, spices, oak, or other solids during secondary. Fruit breaks down and drops sediment over time. Spices in a brew bag can release fine particles. Oak chips or spirals can leave debris behind. All of that settles, and the longer it sits on the lees, the more chance it has to affect flavor.

The clearest sign that a re-rack is needed is a visible layer of sediment. I also check clarity over time. If the mead was clearing and then seems to stop getting brighter, another transfer can move it off the settled debris and restart the clearing process.

I do not rack just because time has passed. If the mead is still clear and there is no new sediment, leaving it alone is usually the better choice. Every transfer introduces some risk of oxidation or contamination, so I only rack when there is a reason.

Common Mistakes

Racking too early is the biggest mistake. If the yeast have not finished, moving the mead can stress them or leave fermentation by-products behind. Wait for stable gravity.

Another mistake is introducing oxygen while racking. Splashing or allowing the mead to free-fall into the new vessel can oxidize the batch, especially once fermentation has slowed and there is no CO2 blanket protecting the liquid. A gentle siphon with the hose near the bottom of the receiving vessel helps minimize splashing.

Some brewers also forget that secondary is not a substitute for good process. If the mead has a flaw from primary, time will not fix it. It might mask it slightly, but the flaw will still be there.

Finally, beginners sometimes add so much fruit or spice in secondary that it becomes difficult to manage. I prefer to add additions in a brew bag or fine-mesh bag so I can pull them out cleanly when the flavor is where I want it.

My Approach

I treat secondary fermentation as the long conditioning and aging phase. The mead goes in once primary is done, and it stays there until it is clear, stable, and tastes ready. That might be a month for a light melomel or six months to a year for a heavier traditional mead. Either way, the secondary vessel is where the mead becomes finished.

The next article covers bottling and back sweetening, the final steps before the mead is ready to drink.

nodes.html:
Primary fermentation is where the yeast turn honey water into mead. It is the busiest phase of the batch, and the decisions you make here will shape almost everything that follows. In this sixth part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will explain what primary fermentation actually is, when to add ingredients to the must, and how to avoid the most common mistake beginners make: moving on too soon.

What Primary Fermentation Is

Primary fermentation is the first stretch after you pitch your yeast. During this phase the yeast consume sugars from the honey and produce ethanol, carbon dioxide, and a range of flavor compounds. In a typical mead, primary fermentation lasts anywhere from one to four weeks, depending on the yeast strain, temperature, starting gravity, and nutrient availability.

The most obvious sign of primary fermentation is bubbling in the airlock. That bubbling is carbon dioxide escaping from the fermenter. Early on it can be aggressive, sometimes pushing foam and liquid through the airlock. After a few days the activity usually settles into a slower, steadier rhythm.

A lot happens below the surface during this phase. Yeast do more than produce alcohol. They also generate esters, phenols, and other aromatic compounds that contribute to the final flavor. They reproduce and build a population large enough to finish the job, and they drop sediment — called lees — as they begin to tire.

Adding Ingredients to Primary

One of the first decisions you will make is whether to add fruit, spices, or other flavorings during primary fermentation or wait until secondary.

Adding additions in primary has some advantages. The yeast activity helps extract color, flavor, and aroma quickly. It can also help sanitize ingredients to a degree, since the active fermentation creates a low-oxygen, acidic environment that discourages many spoilage microbes. Some brewers add fruit in primary for a more integrated, fermented-fruit character.

There are downsides too. The vigorous CO2 production can scrub away delicate volatile aromatics, especially from lighter ingredients like flowers or subtle spices. Fruit added in primary will often lose its fresh character and take on a more cooked or wine-like quality. Yeast can also settle into fruit pieces, making racking and cleanup more difficult.

I generally keep primary simple. Honey, water, yeast, and nutrients go into the fermenter. If I want a strong integrated fruit character — for example, in a berry melomel — I might add the fruit in primary. For delicate additions like rose petals, hibiscus, or spices, I prefer secondary. That gives me more control and preserves the qualities I am after.

Temperature, Oxygen, and Nutrients

Temperature is one of the biggest factors in how a mead ferments. Each yeast strain has a preferred range, and staying inside it matters. Too cold and fermentation can stall or produce sulfur aromas. Too warm and the yeast may create fusel alcohols and harsh flavors that take months to age out. I keep my primary fermenter in a stable spot, away from direct sunlight and big temperature swings.

Yeast also need oxygen early in fermentation. For the first few days, I aerate the must by swirling the fermenter or using a sanitized whisk to introduce oxygen. This helps the yeast build a healthy population. Once fermentation is active, I stop adding oxygen and keep the airlock in place. Oxygen after that point can oxidize the mead and create off-flavors.

Nutrition is just as important. Honey is low in nitrogen and minerals, so I use Go-Ferm during rehydration and add Fermaid O or Fermaid K in stages during primary. The first addition usually goes at pitch, the second about 24 hours later, and the third around the one-third sugar depletion point. If I miss this and the ferment starts smelling like rotten eggs, I add more nutrient right away and degas gently.

When Primary Fermentation Is Actually Over

This is the part where patience pays off. The airlock is not a reliable indicator on its own. Bubbles may slow down or stop long before the yeast are finished, especially in a cooler room where fermentation happens more slowly. The yeast may still be working through the remaining sugars, just without producing visible bubbles.

Even when the airlock looks completely still, the yeast may be in a cleanup phase. After the bulk of sugar consumption, yeast continue to metabolize byproducts and improve the flavor of the mead. Moving the batch off the yeast too early can leave off-flavors behind or stall the fermentation before it is truly finished.

The best way to know primary is done is to take gravity readings with a hydrometer. When the specific gravity is stable across two or three readings taken over several days, the yeast have likely stopped consuming sugar. Only then do I consider racking to secondary.

I also pay attention to the visual cues. The foam cap, if there was one, will have collapsed. The must will look clearer as yeast begin to settle. The sediment layer at the bottom will be thickening. Those signs, combined with stable gravity, tell me the yeast are winding down.

Final Gravity and Estimating ABV

When I decide primary fermentation is over, I take one last gravity reading just before racking to secondary. This is the final gravity, or FG. Comparing it to the original gravity tells me how much sugar the yeast consumed and gives a reasonable estimate of the alcohol by volume.

A hydrometer measures the density of the must compared to water. Sugars make the must denser, so fresh honey water reads high — often around 1.080 to 1.120 for a standard mead. As yeast consume sugar, the gravity drops. A dry traditional mead may finish near 1.000 or slightly below, while a sweet or sack mead finishes higher because residual sugar remains.

The simple homebrew formula is:

Estimated ABV = (OG − FG) × 131.25

The number 131.25 comes from the chemistry of fermentation. When yeast consume sugar, each gram of sugar produces a predictable amount of alcohol and CO₂. The factor 131.25 is a rounded empirical constant that converts the gravity drop — how much denser the must was than water at the start versus at the end — into an approximate alcohol percentage. It is not exact for every must because different sugars, yeast strains, and fermentation conditions change the conversion slightly, but it is accurate enough for home mead making.

For example, if the OG was 1.100 and the FG is 1.010:

(1.100 − 1.010) × 131.25 = 11.81% ABV

If the mead finished sweeter at 1.030:

(1.100 − 1.030) × 131.25 = 9.19% ABV

I record both readings in my brewing log. This estimate is close enough to know what you are pouring and to compare batches over time.

My Process

I let primary run until gravity is stable for at least three days. I do not rush it, and I do not move the batch just because the airlock has gone quiet. Once the readings hold steady, I take a final gravity reading, estimate the ABV, and rack the mead off the lees and into secondary.

The biggest lesson I have learned is that fermentation has its own timeline. The yeast are not watching the calendar. Trust the hydrometer, trust your eyes, and give the yeast time to finish their work.

nodes.html:
At its simplest, mead is just honey, water, and yeast. Those three ingredients will ferment into alcohol on their own, but the choices you make within each category are what shape the final glass. In this fourth part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will walk through the ingredients I work with, the yeast strains I reach for, and the additions that can push a basic mead into something colorful and complex.

Honey

Honey is the heart of mead, and the type you choose matters more than many beginners realize. Different honeys carry different floral, fruity, earthy, or spicy notes based on what the bees were feeding on.

I usually keep a few varieties on hand. Clover honey is mild, affordable, and easy to find, which makes it a good baseline for a traditional mead. Orange blossom honey brings a bright, citrusy quality that works beautifully in lighter batches. Wildflower honey is less predictable, but that unpredictability can be fun — it changes depending on the season and region it came from. Buckwheat honey is dark, robust, and almost molasses-like; a little goes a long way.

You do not need raw honey, but avoid anything with added sugar or syrup. The honey should be 100% honey. Pasteurized honey ferments just fine, and some mead makers even prefer it because it can be more consistent from batch to batch.

Yeast

Yeast is where a lot of the magic happens. There are hundreds of strains to experiment with, and the same honey must fermented with two different yeasts can taste completely different. Some yeasts produce clean, neutral profiles that let the honey shine. Others throw off esters that add fruity, spicy, or floral notes.

For a beginner traditional mead, a neutral wine yeast like Lalvin D-47 or EC-1118 is a reliable place to start. D-47 tends to leave a little more body and works well with traditional and melomel styles, but it prefers cooler temperatures around 62–68°F. If it ferments too warm it can produce harsh, fusel alcohols that take a long time to age out. EC-1118 is a workhorse: it ferments cleanly, tolerates a wider temperature range, and can handle higher alcohol levels.

If you want more character, try an ale yeast or a saison strain. Those can add spice, fruit, or rustic notes that change the whole personality of the batch. Mead yeasts from companies like Mangrove Jack's or White Labs are also worth exploring once you are comfortable with the basics.

Pay attention to the temperature range printed on your yeast packet. A steady temperature inside that range usually produces a cleaner mead than one that swings between warm days and cool nights.

The key takeaway is that yeast is not just a tool for making alcohol. It is an ingredient that shapes aroma, body, and finish.

Water

Water makes up most of the must, so it deserves a mention. I use filtered tap water for most batches. If your tap water has a strong chlorine or sulfur character, let it sit out overnight or use a carbon filter. Distilled or reverse-osmosis water is fine too, though it is so stripped of minerals that you may want to add a small amount of yeast nutrient to help fermentation along.

Additions for Flavor and Color

One of the best parts of making mead is how easy it is to customize. Additions can be introduced in the primary fermenter, during secondary, or even right before bottling.

Fruit is the most common addition. Berries, stone fruit, citrus, and tropical fruit all bring sugar, acid, and color. Adding them in secondary tends to preserve more fresh flavor than adding them at the start, where fermentation can blow off some of the more delicate aromatics.

For color, look beyond fruit. Rose petals can give a soft pink hue and a floral note. Hibiscus adds a vivid red color and a tart, cranberry-like quality. Butterfly pea flower changes color depending on pH and can shift from blue to purple to pink. Elderberries or blackberries can deepen a mead into a rich, wine-like color while adding tannins and depth.

Herbs and spices are another route. Cinnamon, cloves, ginger, vanilla, and cardamom are classic choices. I tend to add spices in secondary using a small muslin bag so I can taste-test and pull them out when the balance feels right.

Even oak can play a role. Oak chips or spirals add structure, tannins, and a hint of vanilla or toast. It is an easy way to make a mead taste more mature without waiting years.

Yeast Nutrition

Honey is nearly all sugar, which means it lacks the nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, and other trace minerals yeast need to stay healthy. Without nutrients, fermentation can stall, produce sulfur or rotten-egg off-flavors, or drag on for months. Good nutrition is what separates a clean mead from a problematic one.

When I rehydrate dried yeast, I use a rehydration nutrient such as Go-Ferm. It gives the yeast a strong start by providing sterols and minerals during rehydration, before the yeast are exposed to the high-sugar must.

During fermentation I add nutrients in stages rather than dumping them all in at the start. The common approach is:

  • At pitch, or within a few hours after pitch.
  • About 24 hours after pitch.
  • Around the one-third sugar depletion point, when roughly one-third of the original sugar has been consumed.

I typically use Fermaid O, Fermaid K, or a blend of organic and inorganic nitrogen. Some brewers also use DAP (diammonium phosphate) early in fermentation, but many prefer to avoid adding DAP after the one-third break because the yeast can no longer take it up effectively.

If I smell rotten eggs or sewage during fermentation, that is usually a sign of nutrient stress. I add more nutrient immediately, gently degas to drive off the gas, and make sure the must is not too cold. Catching it early usually saves the batch.

My Approach

I keep my first few batches simple — good honey, clean water, and a reliable yeast. Once I know the base is sound, I start experimenting with one addition at a time. That way, when something works, I know exactly what caused it. Mead is forgiving, but it rewards patience and small, deliberate changes.

nodes.html:
Before the yeast take over, you have to create the environment they will live in. That mixture of honey, water, and anything else you add before fermentation is called the must. Preparing it well makes the rest of the batch easier, from the first bubble in the airlock to the final gravity reading.

In this part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will walk through how I mix the must, make sure the ingredients are fully combined, and take the first gravity reading with a hydrometer.

Mixing the Must

The basic ratio is simple: honey diluted with water. A common starting point for a one-gallon traditional mead is about two to three pounds of honey per gallon of total volume. More honey means a higher starting gravity, more potential alcohol, and usually a sweeter finish if the yeast do not ferment it all. Less honey gives a lighter, lower-alcohol mead that may finish dry.

I warm the honey container briefly if it has crystallized, but I do not boil it. Boiling drives off delicate aromatics and can darken the honey. A warm water bath is enough to make it pourable. I add the honey to my fermenter first, then pour in about half the water, and stir until the honey is fully dissolved. Once it is mixed, I top up with the rest of the water to reach my target volume.

If I am adding fruit, spices, or other solids, I usually add them to the fermenter before the liquid so they are easier to distribute. For delicate ingredients like rose petals or tea, I sometimes make a strong tea or tincture separately and add it to the must instead of adding the raw plant matter directly.

Combining Everything Thoroughly

Honey is denser than water, so it can settle at the bottom of the fermenter even after it looks mixed. An uneven must will ferment unevenly, and a hydrometer reading taken from the top may read lower than a sample from the bottom. I take the time to stir well, scraping along the bottom of the fermenter to make sure no honey is clinging there.

I also make sure anything else in the fermenter is evenly distributed. Fruit should be submerged or floating uniformly. Spices in a bag should be moved around so they are not clumped in one spot. The goal is a must where a sample taken from any depth gives the same reading.

This is also the best time to add oxygen. I sometimes seal the fermenter and shake it vigorously for a minute or two, or I stir it hard enough to splash. Yeast need oxygen at the start of fermentation to build healthy cell membranes and reproduce. Once fermentation is active, oxygen becomes the enemy because it can oxidize the mead and create off-flavors. So I take advantage of this moment: shake, stir, or whisk the must aggressively now, then seal it up and leave it alone for the rest of fermentation.

Taking an Original Gravity Reading

A hydrometer is the most important tool at this stage. It measures how dense the must is compared to water, and that density comes almost entirely from dissolved sugar. The reading you take now is your original gravity, or OG. It is the baseline you will compare against later to know when fermentation is finished and to estimate alcohol content.

To take a reading, I use the hydrometer cylinder that came with my hydrometer. Everything is sanitized before it touches the must — the cylinder, the hydrometer, and any spoon or tool I use to stir. I lower the hydrometer into the cylinder first, then pour the must into the cylinder until the hydrometer floats freely without touching the bottom. This prevents overflow and gives enough liquid for an accurate reading.

The hydrometer floats higher in denser liquid. I read the number where the liquid surface crosses the scale, making sure the hydrometer is not touching the sides of the cylinder and that no bubbles are clinging to it. Bubbles will lift the hydrometer and give a falsely high reading, so I give it a quick spin to shake them off.

Once I have the reading, I pour the sample back into the fermenter carefully, letting it run down the side to avoid splashing. Since everything was sanitized, there is no reason to waste the must. The only thing I watch for is oxidation — I pour gently and do not agitate the must once fermentation is underway.

For a standard mead, an OG around 1.080 to 1.110 is common. A lighter session mead might start at 1.040 to 1.060. A strong sack mead can start at 1.120 or higher.

The gravity number itself does not tell you the alcohol content yet. It tells you how much sugar is available for the yeast to convert. When fermentation is done, you will take a final gravity reading and compare the two. The larger the drop, the more sugar was consumed, and the higher the alcohol percentage will be.

I always return the sample to the fermenter if it is still clean and fresh. Wasting a cup of mead on readings adds up over a one-gallon batch.

My Approach

I keep must preparation simple and methodical. I measure the honey by weight, mix thoroughly, and take an OG reading before pitching yeast. Those few steps take maybe fifteen minutes, but they give me the numbers I need to track fermentation and the consistency I need for repeatable batches.

The next article covers primary fermentation: what the yeast are doing, how to tell when they are finished, and why patience matters more than the calendar.

nodes.html:
Brewing is 80% cleaning. That joke gets repeated because it is true — the time you spend washing, scrubbing, and sanitizing will dwarf the time you spend pouring honey into water. In this third part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will explain why that work matters, how cleaning and sanitizing are different, and the routine I follow on brew day.

Why Sanitization Matters for Mead

Mead is essentially honey water with yeast, which makes it an inviting environment for microbes. Wild yeast and bacteria live on fruit, in the air, and on anything that touches your brew. If they get a foothold before your chosen yeast takes over, they can produce off-flavors, sour the batch, or turn it into vinegar. Sanitization is the step that tilts the odds in your yeast’s favor by reducing competing organisms to a level your yeast can outpace.

It is worth being honest here: you can sometimes get away with sloppy sanitation and still end up with drinkable mead. Honey must is not as bacteria-friendly as wort, and many wild yeasts are less aggressive than brewing strains. But “sometimes” is not a great brewing strategy. Consistent sanitation is what turns a lucky batch into a reliable process.

Cleaner vs. Sanitizer

Cleaning and sanitizing are related, but they are not the same job, and mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Cleaning is the removal of visible dirt, organic residue, and biofilm. A cleaner lifts honey residue, fruit pulp, oils, and dried yeast off the surface of your gear so water can rinse it away. If you skip cleaning, the sanitizer you apply next will not reach every surface; it will sit on top of the grime instead.

Sanitizing happens after cleaning. A sanitizer reduces the number of microorganisms on a clean surface to a level that will not harm your fermentation. It does not sterilize your equipment, and it does not remove physical debris. That is why you cannot sanitize your way out of poor cleaning.

Think of it this way: cleaning is washing the dishes, sanitizing is making sure the plate is safe to eat from after it is dry. You need both, in that order.

What I Use

For cleaning equipment, a lot of brewers recommend PBW (Powdered Brewery Wash). It’s an alkali cleaner made specifically for breaking down organic residue like honey, fruit pulp, and yeast film. I started with PBW but burned through it quickly—brewing involves a surprising amount of cleaning, and the cost adds up fast.

I’ve since switched to unscented OxiClean Free & Clear as my cleaner. It does the same basic job for a fraction of the price, though it requires extensive rinsing to make sure no residue is left behind. If you’re willing to put in the rinse time, it’s far more cost effective than PBW.

Sanitizing is a separate step, and for that I use StarSan. It’s an acid-based no-rinse sanitizer that kills off wild yeast and bacteria without you having to rinse it out afterward. If you buy the 32 oz version, it lasts for years of brewing because you dilute it to a tiny concentration. And yes—don’t fear the foam. The foam left behind by StarSan is harmless and actually protects your clean surface right up until you add the mead.

My Brew Day Cleaning Routine

I clean in batches, and the kitchen sink is my workstation. I start by filling one side with hot water and OxiClean, then drop in whatever gear I am not actively using—fermenters, airlocks, rubber stoppers, measuring cups, spoons, and the hydrometer test jar. I let them soak for about five minutes while I weigh ingredients or mix the must.

After the soak I pull each item out and scrub it. Sponges handle the wide surfaces, and bottle brushes get into airlock chambers, tubing, and the necks of jugs. Anything with dried-on residue gets an extra minute of attention. Once I am done scrubbing, I rinse everything thoroughly under running water. OxiClean works well, but it needs to be completely rinsed away or it can leave a residue behind.

When the last piece is clean, I drain the sink and rinse it out well. I do not want leftover cleaner weakening my sanitizer. Then I refill the sink with water and StarSan. I do not sanitize everything at once; instead, I drop gear into the sanitizer as I need it. If I know the next step involves the hydrometer, the test jar goes in a few minutes early. When it is time to rack, the auto-siphon and tubing get a soak right before I use them.

Once an item comes out of the StarSan, I do not rinse it with water. The foam and thin film left behind are harmless, and rinsing would just reintroduce whatever is in the tap water. I shake off the excess, use the gear, and move on.

Common Mistakes

The biggest mistake I see is treating sanitizer like a cleaner. Spraying StarSan on a fermenter that still has dried honey or yeast residue does almost nothing; the sanitizer cannot reach the surface underneath the grime. Clean first, then sanitize.

Another common slip is skipping contact time. Sanitizers need a minute or two on the surface to do their job. Dunking an airlock in StarSan and immediately pulling it out is better than nothing, but it is not as reliable as letting it sit for a couple of minutes.

Using scented cleaners is a subtler error. Scented dish soap and laundry detergent can leave fragrances and residues behind that affect aroma and flavor. Stick to unscented products for anything that touches your mead.

A fourth mistake is making StarSan with tap water that has high mineral content. Hard water can make the solution cloudy, and while cloudiness does not always mean it is ineffective, it can reduce the useful life of the batch. If your tap water is very hard, using distilled or reverse-osmosis water helps the sanitizer stay stable longer.

Finally, do not fear the foam. Beginners sometimes rinse StarSan foam out of fear that it will ruin the batch. That foam is harmless, and the no-rinse label means exactly what it says. Rinsing after sanitizing just reintroduces whatever organisms are in your rinse water.

nodes.html:
Mead is one of the easiest ways to start fermenting at home. At its most basic, all you need is honey, water, and yeast. A one-gallon juice jug with a piece of paper towel held over the top by a rubber band will make perfectly drinkable mead.

But if you want a clean, repeatable process, a few pieces of equipment make life much easier. This is the second part of a series that walks through making your first mead from start to finish. In this article I will cover the gear you actually need for a one-gallon batch, point out where you can save money, and flag the few upgrades worth making once you know you enjoy the hobby.

The Bare Minimum

You can make a drinkable one-gallon batch with just a few things. None of them are exotic.

A Fermenter

For one-gallon batches a glass gallon jug works, but I recommend starting with a 1.4–1.5 gallon fermentation vessel instead. The extra headspace catches the foam from active fermentation and makes temperature swings less dramatic. It also means you are not mopping krausen off your floor because you cut the headspace too close.

Glass fermenters are easy to find used at tag sales and thrift stores for a few dollars, and glass can be cleaned and reused almost indefinitely. Do not shy away from a used glass vessel as long as you inspect it for chips and clean it thoroughly before your first batch.

I highly recommend the Little Big Mouth Bubbler from Northern Brewer. It holds 1.4 gallons, has a wide mouth that actually fits a hand and a sponge, and is easy to clean without specialized brushes. At the time of writing it sells for $22.99. Get the plain version without the spigot — you do not need the spout for transferring liquid. I bought one with the spout, and over time I have regretted it; the spigot adds a place for leaks and gunk to hide, and a simple siphon is more reliable anyway.

The wide mouth is especially useful if you plan to add fruit during primary or secondary fermentation. Fishing chunks of fruit out of a narrow-neck jug is not something you want to do more than once.

An Airlock and Stopper

An airlock lets CO₂ escape while keeping oxygen and wild yeast out. I use one at every step, from primary fermentation through secondary fermentation, right up until bottling day.

I keep a Fastrack 10‑Pack Airlocks on hand. A 10‑pack is inexpensive enough that I am not worried if one gets lost or cracked mid‑batch, and they work fine for both primary and secondary fermentations.

Pay attention to the bung size your fermenter needs. The Little Big Mouth Bubbler takes a drilled size 5 bung, so make sure whatever stopper you order matches that spec. A size too small will leak; a size too large will fight you every time you sanitize and insert it. Different fermenters require different bung sizes, so whenever you buy a new fermenter, pick up several extra bungs in the matching size at the same time. They are cheap and easy to misplace, and you will not want to delay a brew day because one rolled under the fridge. The North Mountain Supply #5.5 drilled rubber stoppers work well and come in a pack of three for about $2.49 at the time of writing.

A Hydrometer

A hydrometer is the only way to accurately measure sugar content before and after fermentation, which lets you calculate ABV. They are fragile and only cost about ten dollars, so buy two while you are ordering.

Get one that comes with a hydrometer cylinder. The cylinder gives you a clean, narrow vessel to float the hydrometer in, which is much easier than trying to read it inside a fermenter full of foam. I like the Brewer's Elite Hydrometer Combo — it includes the hydrometer, a cylinder, and a hard case for about $21.99 at the time of writing.

You also need a way to fill that cylinder without making a mess. The best method I have found is a simple turkey baster — draw a sample from the fermenter, squirt it into the cylinder, and sanitize it just like everything else. You can pick one up cheap from almost anywhere.

Pour gravity samples back into the fermenter carefully to avoid oxidation.

A Racking Cane and Siphon Tubing

You need to move mead from the fermenter to bottles without dumping the yeast sediment in. A simple auto-siphon is easier than trying to start a siphon with your mouth, and it gives you much more control over what you transfer.

The Fermtech Mini Auto-Siphon is about $15.99 at the time of writing and is a game changer when moving mead from primary to secondary fermentation. This one is sized for small batches. If you ever scale up to larger volumes you will want a larger siphon.

For a cleaner setup that handles both the transfer and the fill in one go, the Dbgogo Auto-Siphon and Bottle Filler Set comes with both the auto-siphon and a bottle-filling wand, which reduces mess and speeds up the whole bottling process.

Bottles and Closures

You can bottle your mead in almost any container you like. Premium wine bottles work beautifully with cork stoppers, and if you do not mind spending a bit, a Portuguese Floor Corker makes the job smooth. I do not cork my bottles myself and I do not own this style of corker yet; I may pick one up down the road as my collection of filled bottles grows, but I have not made that move so far.

For the ultra-budget minded, reusable beer bottles are perfectly fine. They are cheap to source, and the capping machine needed to seal them is typically under $20. A hand capper like the WENNING Bottle Capping Machine will handle crown caps without much fuss. Do not use twist-off bottles — the caps will not seal well and you will end up with flat mead.

I personally stick with a set of swing-top bottles that come in a few different sizes. The eispap swing-top bottles are about $23.99 at the time of writing. I mostly make still meads, so the swing-top seal is plenty strong for my needs. If I do bottle carbonate, I use crown caps and normal bottles because the pressure needs a stronger seal.

For a one-gallon batch you will fill about four of those swing-top bottles. If you are anything like me and want plenty of bottles in backup, you will want to buy a lot of them, and that is where a lot of the expense hides. I personally have eight large bottles and six small bottles on hand and still feel like I need about six times more than that.

Secondary Fermentation Vessels

After primary fermentation I transfer the mead into a clean vessel for secondary fermentation. This is the long conditioning and aging step where the mead clears and the flavors mellow. The vessel stays sealed with an airlock or rubber stopper.

I keep two different vessels on hand for secondary fermentation. When I want to add fruit, spices, or oak, I use a wide‑mouth fermenter because the opening makes it easy to get additions in and out. For plain traditional meads that just need to clear, I use 1‑gallon glass jugs from North Mountain Supply. They are about $14.99 each at the time of writing.

Each of these jars needs its own airlock and drilled bung so gas can escape while the mead ages. I highly suggest looping a rubber band over the airlock and then around the handle on the neck of the jar to keep the airlock from working itself loose, especially when a jar sits untouched for months.

If you plan to keep more than one batch going at once, you will need a lot of these. Meads can sit in secondary fermentation for several months, and some stay there for a year or more. Having enough jars lets you keep several batches conditioning in secondary while still having free vessels for new primary fermentations.

The Nice-to-Haves

Once you know you like mead making, a few purchases make life easier.

Thermometer: Fermentation temperature matters. A stick-on thermometer on your fermenter gives you a quick reading. An inexpensive digital probe is useful if you are rehydrating yeast or adjusting must temperature.

Kitchen scale: Measuring ingredients by weight is more accurate than volume, especially for honey and additives. Pick one that can handle the weight of a full fermenter if you plan to set the vessel right on the scale and use the tare function. I use the Escali Primo Digital Kitchen Scale.

Funnel: A funnel with a strainer helps transfer must into a glass jug without spilling or clogging the neck.

Measuring cups and spoons: Get your own set early on. If you share a kitchen, your partner will get tired of you borrowing their tools.

What You Can Skip

  • A kegging setup. Bottling is tedious but free if you save bottles. Kegging is great, but it gets expensive fast. A five-gallon Cornelius keg runs about $100–$130 each, and on top of that you need a CO₂ tank, a regulator, tubing, taps, connectors, a temperature controller if you convert a freezer into a keezer, and the freezer itself. It can quickly add up to $1,000–$2,000. It is not required to make good mead.

  • A dedicated fermentation fridge. Temperature control matters for clean fermentation, but you can manage early batches by brewing styles that match your ambient temperature, or by using a swamp cooler setup with a tub of water and frozen bottles. I ferment primary on my kitchen counter at room temperature, which does fluctuate. Secondary aging jars sit on the same counter, out of direct sunlight but still in ambient light. At some point I really do need to set up a fermentation station, but I do not have the time or money for that right now.

  • Fancy pH meters and lab gear. Useful later, completely unnecessary for your first few batches.

What This Actually Costs

Here is a realistic breakdown for a complete starter setup:

Core essentials (~$80):

  • Fermenter (Little Big Mouth Bubbler): $23
  • Airlocks (10‑pack) and stoppers: $10
  • Hydrometer with cylinder: $22
  • Turkey baster: $7
  • Mini auto-siphon: $16

Bottling options:

Budget route (~$100 total): Reuse non-twist-off beer bottles and buy a bag of crown caps ($5–10). Add a handheld capper ($19) if you do not own one.

Swing-top route (~$145 total): Buy a set of swing-top bottles ($24) and get 2–3 sets for backups. This saves time on bottling day and works great for still meads.

Secondary fermentation vessels (~$15 each): Add one or two 1-gallon glass jugs if you plan to age or clear your mead separately. If you keep multiple batches going, you will want several.

Nice-to-haves (~$50–75): Kitchen scale ($25–35), stick-on thermometer ($10), funnel ($10), dedicated measuring cups and spoons ($15).

You can absolutely start for under $100 by borrowing kitchen tools, using saved bottles, and skipping the nice-to-haves. Or you can spend $200+ for a complete setup with backups and secondary vessels. Both approaches make the same mead.

The best tool in your brewery is patience. The second best is a notebook.

series.description: A complete beginner's guide to making mead at home, from equipment and ingredients through fermentation, back-sweetening, pasteurization, and bottling.

nodes.html:
Before you mix your first must, it helps to know what kind of mead you are aiming for. Mead is much broader than "honey wine." Change the honey, add fruit, introduce smoke or chilies, or ferment the same recipe dry instead of sweet, and you end up with a different style entirely. In this first part of the Intro to Making Mead series I will walk through the main categories, what defines each one, and where I think a beginner should start.

Traditional Mead

This is the baseline: honey, water, and yeast, with no fruit, spices, or other flavoring ingredients added. What you taste is what the honey and yeast created together. A traditional mead can be dry, semi-sweet, or sweet, and it can be still or sparkling, but the core requirement is that honey character carries the show.

Traditional meads are the best place to learn how your yeast and honey choices shape the final glass. Without fruit or spice to hide behind, every decision matters.

Melomel

A melomel is any mead made with fruit. Berries, stone fruit, tropical fruit, and even dried fruit all count. The fruit contributes sugar, acid, tannin, and color, which makes melomels more forgiving than traditional meads — the fruit can smooth out rough edges in a young batch.

Within melomel there are a few common sub-styles:

  • Cyser — mead made with apple juice or cider instead of some or all of the water. It sits somewhere between mead and cider.
  • Pyment — mead made with grape juice. It can taste like a honey-kissed white or red wine depending on the grapes.
  • Blackberry, cherry, strawberry, blueberry meads — these are all melomels, even if people rarely use the umbrella term.

I make a lot of melomels because fruit gives the batch instant personality.

Metheglin

Metheglin is mead made with spices, herbs, or both. Cinnamon, cloves, ginger, vanilla, cardamom, chamomile, and lavender are common choices. The name comes from an old Welsh word for spiced mead, and the style is a great way to experiment once you are comfortable with a basic ferment.

The trick with metheglin is restraint. A little spice goes a long way in mead, and it is much easier to add more later than to remove too much.

Braggot

Braggot is a hybrid of mead and beer. It is made with both honey and malted grain, and it is usually hopped. The malt contributes body, color, and bready or caramel notes, while the honey keeps the finish lighter and adds floral or fruity character.

I have not brewed a braggot myself yet, but it is on my list. If you come from a beer-brewing background, this style is a natural bridge into mead.

Bochet

Bochet is made by caramelizing the honey before fermentation. Heating honey darkens it, deepens the flavor, and introduces notes of toffee, marshmallow, dark fruit, and even a slight bitterness. A bochet can be a traditional mead, a melomel, or a metheglin — the caramelized honey is what defines it.

Bochet takes extra care because hot honey expands and can boil over violently. It is not a beginner process, but the results can be stunning.

Capsicumel / Capsumel

Capsicumel, sometimes written capsumel, is mead flavored with peppers — usually chili peppers. The heat can range from a gentle warmth to genuinely spicy, and the pepper flavor is usually balanced with fruit, smoke, or honey sweetness.

I have not brewed one yet, but I am fascinated by them. Capsicumels are a great example of how flexible mead can be; the honey base supports flavors that would fight each other in other beverages.

Hydromel / Session Mead

A hydromel is a lower-alcohol mead, often in the 3.5% to 7% ABV range. The name comes from the Greek root for water, and the style is intentionally light, crisp, and drinkable. Session meads are usually carbonated and served cold, more like a hard cider or sparkling wine than a heavy dessert mead.

Hydromels are a good choice if you want something refreshing and do not want to wait months for a high-ABV batch to mellow.

Sack Mead / Dessert Mead

At the opposite end of the spectrum, sack mead is strong and sweet, typically 14% ABV or higher with plenty of residual honey left in the finished product. The higher alcohol and sugar make it rich, warming, and suited to small pours after dinner.

Sack meads take patience. They often need a year or more of aging before the alcohol heat mellows and the flavors integrate.

Sparkling Mead

Any of the styles above can be sparkling. Carbonation adds mouthfeel, lifts aromatics, and can make a dry mead feel more complete. Sparkling meads are bottled with a small amount of priming sugar and allowed to carbonate naturally, or they are force-carbonated in a keg.

I usually bottle still meads, but I have been tempted to try force-carbonating a session hydromel.

Smoked and Specialty Meads

Beyond the classic categories, mead makers add everything from coffee and chocolate to flowers, tea, and smoke. A bochet with smoked malt becomes something close to a braggot-bochet hybrid. A metheglin with lapsang souchong tea picks up a campfire quality. There is no firm style name for every combination, and that is part of the fun.

When you move into specialty territory, the best approach is to pick one dominant flavor idea and build the rest of the recipe around it.

Where to Start

If this is your first batch, I recommend a traditional mead or a simple melomel. Both teach you how honey, yeast, water, and time interact, and they give you a baseline to compare against when you start experimenting. A traditional mead will show you exactly what your yeast and honey contributed. A melomel with berries or cherries will be more forgiving and usually ready to drink a little sooner.

Once you have a few batches under your belt, try a metheglin, experiment with a bochet, or split a batch in secondary to test two different flavor additions side by side.

The rest of this series will cover the equipment, cleaning routine, ingredients, and fermentation process you need to turn any of these styles into a finished batch.

nodes.html:
Bottling is the most rewarding—and potentially most stressful—part of the brewing process. After weeks of waiting, your brew finally moves from the fermenter into its final home. It is also the stage where a few careless mistakes can turn a promising batch into broken glass and a sticky floor, so I treat it with the same care as the earlier steps.

The Setup: Getting the Liquid into the Bottle

There are several ways to approach bottling, and the "right" one usually depends on your gear and your tolerance for mess.

The Spigot and Hose

If your fermenter has a built-in spigot, the simplest path is to attach a food-grade hose and run it directly into each bottle. The main drawback is flow control: the liquid keeps moving whenever the spigot is open, so you often lose product while shifting the hose from bottle to bottle. Technically, you can close the spigot between bottles, but I try to avoid that. The spigot sits close to the lees at the bottom, and repeatedly opening and closing it tends to stir up sediment and cloud the finished brew.

The Auto-Siphon and Bottle Filler

For a cleaner operation, I use an auto-siphon to move liquid out of the fermenter, connected to a bottle-filling wand that controls flow into each bottle. The wand has a small plastic tip at the bottom that acts like a valve: press it against the bottom of a bottle and liquid flows; lift it and the flow stops. This lets me move from bottle to bottle with minimal waste, losing only a drop or two rather than a stream of mead or wine.

The Critical Safety Check: Avoiding "Bottle Bombs"

Before a single drop enters a bottle, you must be certain fermentation is finished. I verify this by taking multiple gravity readings over several days until the number is stable. If the yeast is still active and you seal it in glass with residual sugar, you risk a bottle bomb — the internal pressure climbs until the bottle fails, sending glass shards and sticky liquid across your storage area.

Once fermentation is confirmed complete, you need to stabilize the brew. I use two different methods, depending on the batch: chemical stabilization with powders, or pasteurization with heat. They are not interchangeable, and each changes the timing of other steps like back-sweetening.

Chemical Stabilization

I add a combination of potassium metabisulfite and potassium sorbate to stop the yeast from restarting fermentation. For a standard one-gallon batch, I use approximately 1/4 teaspoon of potassium metabisulfite and 1/2 teaspoon of potassium sorbate. The metabisulfite works as an antioxidant and antimicrobial, while the sorbate keeps any remaining yeast cells from multiplying. I mix them in thoroughly and wait at least 24 hours before adding more sugar or bottling.

Pasteurization

The other reliable method is pasteurization, which uses heat to neutralize the yeast. When I choose this route, I follow the most common homebrewing standards: hold the bottles at either 140°F for 20 minutes or 160°F for 1 minute.

The key detail is that these temperatures must be the internal temperature of the liquid, not just the water surrounding the bottles. I use my all-in-one Clawhammer supply system to heat water to 160°F, then set the bottles in my grain basket. That setup lets me stick a thermometer directly into one of the bottles so I can track the actual liquid temperature and stop the process once the target is reached, without boiling the brew.

Back-sweetening

If the finished brew tastes too dry, you can back-sweeten with honey or another sugar source. Timing matters here, because adding sugar to active yeast will restart fermentation.

When using Potassium Sorbate + Potassium Metabisulfite:

Fermentation finishes → Rack off the lees → Add stabilizers → Wait 24–48 hours → Back-sweeten → Verify stability → Bottle.

When using Pasteurization:

Fermentation finishes → Back-sweeten → Allow honey to fully dissolve and mix → Pasteurize → Cool → Bottle.

The critical distinction: do not rely on potassium sorbate alone. The sorbate and metabisulfite work together, and neither replaces the need to confirm fermentation is truly finished before you add more sugar.

Bottle Carbonation with Crown Caps

If you want a sparkling finish, you can bottle carbonate using standard beer bottles and crown caps. Carbonation requires leaving a precise amount of residual sugar — called priming sugar — in the liquid. The yeast consumes that sugar inside the sealed bottle and produces CO2 that dissolves into the brew.

Using crown caps is the gold standard here because they form a true airtight seal that can withstand the high pressures involved. For a single 12-ounce bottle, I target about 2 grams of white sugar (roughly 1/2 teaspoon), scaling proportionally for larger bottles.

There are many calculators available to determine the exact amount of priming sugar based on your volume and desired carbonation level. One tool I have used is the Brewers Friend Priming Calculator.

Some brewers add sugar to each bottle individually; others dissolve the full amount in the bulk container before bottling. If you use the bulk method, make sure the sugar is fully dissolved and evenly mixed before you start siphoning, or you will end up with some bottles flat and others over-carbonated.

Whichever route you choose, keep your priming calculations exact. Too little sugar and the brew is flat; too much and you are back to the "bottle bomb" scenario.

nodes.html:
I bought a Tilt Hydrometer because the idea of watching fermentation gravity from my phone sounded like the future. No more sanitizing a wine thief, no more sticky hydrometer cylinders, no more guessing when a batch had stalled. Just drop the device into the must, open the app, and watch the numbers roll in. In practice, that fantasy is about seventy percent real.

What the Tilt Does Well

The Tilt really is clever. It is a sealed, floating hydrometer and thermometer that broadcasts gravity and temperature over Bluetooth. Sanitize it, drop it in, and it starts logging. For someone who makes mead and wine in small batches, the convenience is meaningful. I can check a fermentation curve from the kitchen table, the office, or even while running errands if I have cloud logging enabled.

Setup is genuinely simple. The device arrives pre-calibrated, and the app finds it quickly. There are no probes to insert, no grommets to wrestle into a lid, and no risk of introducing oxygen every time I want a reading. That alone makes it attractive for long secondary ferments where you want to peek without disturbing anything.

Tilt also offers the units in multiple colors, which is genuinely useful if you run more than one fermenter at a time. Each color shows up as its own device in the app, so I can tell at a glance which bucket is which. For a small-scale home brewer juggling a couple of projects, that little detail matters.

The Caveats I Did Not Expect

For all the polish in the marketing, the day-to-day experience has rough edges. The first one showed up before I even brewed with it: the battery drains on the shelf. I store my Tilt upright, sideways, and every other orientation people suggest online, and it still shows up weaker than I expect the next time I need it. It is not a dealbreaker because the battery is replaceable, but it is annoying for a device whose whole pitch is readiness.

The second issue is specific to beer, and it is the one that makes me hesitate before dropping the Tilt into a hoppy or high-protein batch. Krausen can build up enough that the Tilt no longer tilts freely. When that happens, the reading lags or flatlines, and you are left trying to decide whether fermentation is done or the device is just stuck against the side of the bucket. In wines and meads with less aggressive foam it has been more reliable, but I have learned not to trust it blindly in the final days of any batch.

One Idea for a Better Design

I have wondered whether a simple mechanical rig could solve the krausen problem. The sketch below is just a thought experiment, not something I have built or tested, but it shows the idea: a small rectangular chassis holds the Tilt on a pivot so it can still rock and measure gravity, while an adjustable cord and a ballast weight keep the whole assembly submerged below the foam layer.

If a design like this kept the sensor below the surface while still allowing it to tilt, it could remove one of the biggest accuracy problems the Tilt has today. Whether Tilt or a third-party accessory maker ever produces something similar is another question entirely.

Then there is the software experience. The data exports to Google Sheets, which works, but it does not feel like a modern product dashboard. Graphs are janky, layout is manual, and there is no beautiful Tilt-owned portal that ties everything together. For a premium brewing accessory, the reporting side feels like an afterthought. I would love a clean web portal with shareable batch timelines, but that does not exist today.

Finally, I simply use it less than I thought I would. For meads and wines, gravity often follows a predictable arc, and once I have a rhythm I do not feel compelled to log every point digitally. I still use the Tilt for experiments or finicky batches, but it is not the default tool I imagined it would be.

Is It Worth Buying?

Honestly, I do not think it is. The Tilt Hydrometer has its strengths, but once you stack the $135 price against the inaccurate readings, the janky graphs, and the general sense that the software has been neglected, it starts to feel like an overpriced gimmick rather than an essential brewing tool.

I worry it is heading the same direction as the PLAATO Airlock, which I also bought. PLAATO looked promising, then the company announced it was shifting focus to commercial breweries and away from consumers. The app stopped getting updates, the cloud service effectively vanished, and the device I paid good money for became a paperweight overnight. It remains one of the worst purchases I have ever made. I look at the Tilt and ask the same question: is the product going to keep improving, or is the consumer side going to be abandoned once the next pivot happens?

Right now the hardware has potential, but the software and ecosystem do not inspire confidence. A small weighted chassis that holds the Tilt below the surface while still letting it tilt freely would solve the krausen-sticking problem almost entirely. If Tilt commits to that kind of hardware refinement and a real reporting platform, this could become a solid investment. Until then, I would not recommend buying one for most homebrewers.

Rating: 3 out of 5 — a neat idea with real utility, but at this price it needs accuracy and software that keep up with the marketing.

frontmatter.excerpt: The Tilt Hydrometer promises 24/7 gravity and temperature readings straight from your fermenter. I wanted to love it, and in some ways I do—but a few persistent flaws keep it from earning a permanent place in every batch.

nodes.html:
My brewing journey started in 2022, though I'd actually started researching the topic during COVID. After falling down countless YouTube rabbit holes, I was pretty knowledgeable on the subject before I ever brewed my first batch.

I've since added a dedicated brewing section to the site where I share recipes for beer, wine, and mead — complete with ingredients, step-by-step instructions, and notes from my own brewing experiences.

Learning From the Pros

I started watching YouTube videos to learn the basics. I call it YouTube Academy — because you can literally learn anything you want from YouTube, and brewing is no exception. Three channels became my go-to resources:

  • Man Made Mead — The definitive guide to all things mead
  • Doin' The Most — Creative recipes and experiments
  • City Steading Brews — Practical brewing for urban dwellers

These creators made brewing approachable. They broke down complex processes into simple steps and showed that you didn't need a massive setup to make great beverages.

The Northern Brewer Starter Kit

Following their recommendations, I bought a 1-gallon mead kit from Northern Brewer. This seems to be the universal entry point for new brewers — and I suspect that's not accidental. Northern Brewer was heavily sponsoring content creators at the time, providing them with tools and ingredients for their videos. Smart marketing, and it definitely worked on me.

The kit arrived with everything I needed to make my first beer: Caribou Slobber, a brown ale extract kit. The beer came out decent, but it wasn't a good first brewing experience. It wasn't really an enjoyable brown ale — and I've enjoyed brown ales in the past.

My second kit was a 1-gallon elderberry mead kit. The mead came out nice, but I messed it up by over-sweetening when I back-sweetened it — the entire batch was ruined. After those experiences, I started thinking about expanding.

Moving to Beer

At this point in my life, I enjoyed drinking beer way more than wine, and mead was an entirely new category for me. I wanted to brew what I actually liked to drink. Beer felt like the logical next step — more complex recipes, more variables to control, and a much wider range of styles to explore.

When I started brewing beer, I turned to a new set of YouTube creators for knowledge:

  • Adam Makes Beer
  • Beer-N-BBQ by Larry
  • Bitter Reality Brewing
  • Cityscape Brewing
  • Clawhammer Supply
  • David Heath Homebrew
  • Don Osborn
  • Exit 12 Homebrew
  • Hops & Gnarly

I also followed these creators who have since stopped making brewing content:

  • Jus' Brewing
  • Party Time Brewing
  • Short Circuited Brewers

Leveling Up

My wonderful wife saw how much I was enjoying the hobby and surprised me with a serious upgrade — a 10 gallon electric brewing system from Clawhammer Supply. This was a massive step up from my 1-gallon stovetop setup. Digital temperature control, built-in pump, and enough capacity to brew real batches that would actually last more than a week.

It was exactly what I needed to take brewing from a fun experiment to a serious hobby.

The Bottling Problem

I was able to brew a batch of beer but had no easy way to store it when finished. I was having to bottle up around 48 bottles of beer after every batch — cleaning, sanitizing, filling, capping, and then finding space to store them all. It turned every brew day into a two-day affair with all the cleanup and bottling.

Bottling is something that I do not miss.

The Honda Dealership Connection

The real pivot point came unexpectedly. We went to our local Honda dealership to trade in our minivan — my wife was done being a soccer mom and wanted an SUV. We ended up driving home in a 2020 Honda Pilot, but that's not the real story here.

While we were there, I struck up a conversation with the sales manager. We got a bit off-topic from the vehicle, and I mentioned I was getting into home brewing. He was surprised — not at the fact that I was a home brewer, but rather that I brought up the topic at his workplace. As it turned out, he was selling a bunch of brewing equipment because he'd lost time for the hobby.

"What do you have?" I asked.

He had a full keezer with kegs, taps, CO₂ tank, regulator — everything I needed to have beer on tap in my kitchen. He also had a beer gun for bottle filling, two large 5-gallon plastic fermenters, and other odds and ends for brewing.

I asked how much he wanted for it. When he said approximately $1,000, I quickly stated that I couldn't take that on along with the vehicle. But looking back, it was well worth what he was asking — a complete setup like that would have cost significantly more buying everything new.

That's when my wife injected herself into the conversation.

"No, you have to buy this," she said firmly. "This is something you have wanted for a while, and opportunities like this do not come up that often."

She was right, of course. I'd been dreaming about having beer on tap at home since I started brewing, but I never thought I'd find a complete setup — especially not from a random conversation at a car dealership.

In the end, we walked out with the vehicle along with a date to pick up the brewing equipment.

What I've Brewed

Over the years I've brewed a few different styles of beer. I started off using an all-grain kit from Northern Brewer but found that shipping delays caused me some issues. Something was happening at Northern Brewer that was causing long delays — I'm not sure what was going on behind the scenes, but waiting weeks for ingredients got frustrating fast.

I ended up switching suppliers shortly after that experience. I started using More Beer, which has never given me any issues over the years. Reliable shipping, good quality ingredients, and their customer service has been solid.

I've made an IPA, a Cream Ale, and a Summer Shandy — but I tend to stick to what I like to brew. Over the years that's been cream ales. They're crisp, clean, refreshing, and a crowd-pleaser when I have friends over. Not too hoppy, not too heavy — just an easy-drinking beer that works year-round.

I'm also planning to try making my own hard seltzer — it's a simple recipe of just corn sugar, water, yeast, and flavoring.

Full Circle

More recently I've had limited time to brew beer. Maybe this time limitation has something to do with it, but I've started making more wine and meads again.

I currently have a Cherry Mead in primary fermentation — a sweet mead with whole frozen cherries added in both primary and secondary for depth of flavor and that beautiful red color.

It's funny how things come full circle. I started with mead, moved to beer when I had the time and equipment, and now find myself back to mead as life gets busier. Different phases, different beverages, same satisfying hobby.

frontmatter.title: My Home Brewing Journey: From Mead to Beer on Tap
frontmatter.excerpt: How I started home brewing in 2022 with a 1-gallon mead kit and ended up with a full keezer setup in my kitchen thanks to a chance encounter at a Honda dealership.
